title: The Room at the End of the Hall
content:
When Clara arrived at Blackwood House, the first thing she noticed was the clock.

It stood at the end of the entrance hall, beneath a portrait of a stern-looking woman whose name had been forgotten by everyone except the family. The clock had stopped at precisely 11:17.

Clara had been hired to catalogue the house's library before it was sold, and she had expected the work to take no more than a week. The house, however, seemed determined to make the task more complicated.

— The electricity works in most of the rooms — said Mr. Bennett, the caretaker, as he handed her the keys. — But don't expect everything to function properly.

Clara glanced toward the clock.

— Does that include this?

The old man followed her gaze.

— That stopped years ago.

— Has anyone tried repairing it?

Mr. Bennett hesitated.

— Not successfully.

Clara smiled politely, assuming there was a story behind the answer.

There was.

She discovered it that evening.

First, she noticed that one of the bookshelves in the library had been moved slightly away from the wall. Then, while trying to push it back into place, she heard a hollow sound behind it.

Clara stopped.

She knocked against the wall.

Nothing.

She knocked again.

This time, there was a faint echo.

She immediately moved the shelf aside.

Behind it was a narrow wooden door.

There was no handle.

She examined the frame carefully and noticed a small brass keyhole.

She searched the desk, the drawers, and the cabinets.

Nothing.

Eventually, she decided to leave it alone.

The next morning, however, the door was open.

Clara stood in front of it for several seconds, unable to explain what she was seeing.

She was certain she had locked the library before going to bed.

She was equally certain that she had not opened the hidden door.

She entered.

First came a narrow passage.

Then a staircase.

Finally, at the top, she found a small room containing nothing but a wooden chair, an empty fireplace, and another clock.

It had stopped at 11:17.

Clara felt a chill.

She walked toward the clock and examined it.

Unlike the one downstairs, this one was still in excellent condition.

She touched the hands.

They moved.

Then she heard footsteps below.

She turned around.

— Hello?

No answer.

She descended the stairs quickly and returned to the library.

Mr. Bennett was standing beside the window.

— You shouldn't have gone up there.

Clara stared at him.

— You knew about the room.

He looked away.

— Everyone who has worked here eventually finds it.

— And nobody thought to mention it?

— The family preferred that we didn't.

— Why?

The caretaker remained silent.

Finally, he said:

— Because of what happened there.

Clara waited.

— Twenty-seven years ago, the youngest daughter disappeared.

The room seemed suddenly colder.

— Disappeared?

— Her name was Eleanor. She was nineteen.

— What happened?

Mr. Bennett sighed.

— She went upstairs one evening. Her father heard her arguing with someone. A few minutes later, he heard a door slam.

— And then?

— Then there was silence.

Clara folded her arms.

— Did they find her?

— No.

— Was there evidence that she had left the house?

— None.

Clara looked toward the hidden door.

— What about that room?

Mr. Bennett shook his head.

— They searched it immediately.

— And?

— Nothing.

Clara spent the rest of the morning searching through the library records. She had originally intended to catalogue the books, but Eleanor's disappearance had become impossible to ignore.

First, she searched for newspaper articles.

Then, she examined family correspondence.

Finally, she found a letter hidden inside an old book.

It was dated three days before Eleanor disappeared.

The letter contained only one sentence.

— If anything happens to me, look behind the clock.

Clara read it twice.

Then she ran upstairs.

The clock in the hidden room stood exactly where she had left it.

She removed it from the wall.

Behind it was a small cavity.

Inside was a metal box.

Her hands trembled as she opened it.

There were photographs, letters, and a diary.

She opened the diary.

Eleanor had written about someone who had been visiting the house secretly. At first, she referred to him only as the stranger. Later, she gave him a name.

Thomas.

Clara continued reading.

Eleanor had discovered that Thomas was not a stranger at all.

He was her father's illegitimate son.

And he wanted his inheritance.

The final pages became increasingly frantic.

— He knows that I found the documents.

— He says nobody will believe me.

— I am going to confront Father tonight.

Then there was one final entry.

— 11:17. He is here.

Clara closed the diary.

For several seconds, she could hear nothing except her own breathing.

Then she noticed something she had missed before.

There was a second door in the room.

She opened it.

Behind it was a narrow staircase leading down into the walls of the house.

At the bottom, she found an old corridor.

It led directly to the cellar.

Clara's heart began racing.

The disappearance had never been a mystery.

Eleanor had not vanished.

She had escaped through the hidden passage.

But where had she gone?

Clara returned to the library and searched the remaining documents.

First, she found Eleanor's birth certificate.

Then, she found a second document.

A marriage certificate.

Eleanor had married Thomas.

Twenty years after her supposed disappearance.

Clara stared at the document in disbelief.

Thomas had not killed her.

He had helped her escape.

But why had they hidden everything?

The answer came from a letter written years later.

Eleanor had discovered that her father intended to have Thomas arrested for theft. She had helped Thomas escape before confronting her father, and together they had disappeared.

The family had concealed the truth to avoid scandal.

Clara was still reading when she heard the front door open downstairs.

She closed the folder.

— Mr. Bennett?

No answer.

She stepped into the hallway.

The clock at the end of the hall was moving.

For the first time in twenty-seven years, its hands were no longer frozen at 11:17.

They moved slowly toward midnight.

Clara walked closer.

Behind the clock, something had been placed recently.

A photograph.

She picked it up.

It showed an elderly woman standing beside an old man in front of a small house.

On the back, someone had written:

— She knew you would eventually find the truth.

Clara turned toward the entrance.

Mr. Bennett was standing there.

He looked at the photograph in her hand and smiled sadly.

— You found her.

Clara stared at him.

— Where is she?

— She died last year.

Clara lowered the photograph.

— And Thomas?

— A few months before her.

— Then why leave this here?

Mr. Bennett looked toward the clock.

— Because Eleanor knew that one day someone would come looking for answers.

Clara looked at the clock again.

It was now midnight.

The bell rang once.

Then again.

And finally, twelve times.

When the last bell faded, the clock stopped.

Not at 11:17 this time.

At midnight.

Clara looked down at the photograph.

For the first time since arriving at Blackwood House, she understood why the old caretaker had never tried to repair the clock.

It had never been broken.

It had simply been waiting.

And now, finally, it had finished telling its story.
